title: Sliding Window Implementation
description: Implement a sliding window rate limiter with exact and approximate algorithms, including Redis sorted sets and weighted counters.

data.text: Sliding window rate limiting eliminates the boundary burst problem of fixed window counting. The exact approach stores every request timestamp in a Redis sorted set. The approximate approach uses weighted counters for O(1) operations. Choose based on your accuracy requirements and memory budget.
Exact Sliding Window with Redis Sorted Sets
Store request timestamps as members in a sorted set scored by time. Count members within the window. Remove expired entries to keep memory bounded.

data.title: Redis sorted set sliding window — exact count
data.content: Every request adds its timestamp to the sorted set. Count entries within the window before deciding.
data.code:
-- KEYS[1] = rate limit key
-- ARGV[1] = window size in seconds (e.g., 60)
-- ARGV[2] = max requests (e.g., 100)
-- ARGV[3] = now in milliseconds

local key = KEYS[1]
local window = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local max_requests = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local window_start = now - (window * 1000)

-- Remove expired entries
redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', key, '-inf', window_start)

-- Count current entries
local count = redis.call('ZCARD', key)

if count < max_requests then
    redis.call('ZADD', key, now, now)
    redis.call('EXPIRE', key, window)
    return {1, max_requests - count - 1, 0}
end

-- Calculate retry after (when oldest entry expires)
local oldest = redis.call('ZRANGE', key, 0, 0)[1]
local retry_after = math.ceil((tonumber(oldest) + window * 1000 - now) / 1000)
return {0, 0, retry_after}

data.text: Approximate Sliding Window with Weighted Counters
Use two counters (previous window and current window) with a weighted blend. This is O(1) and eliminates most boundary burst without storing individual timestamps.

data.title: Approximate sliding window in Redis hash
data.content: Store two counters and rotate the window when it expires.
data.code:
-- KEYS[1] = rate limit key
-- ARGV[1] = window size in seconds
-- ARGV[2] = max requests
-- ARGV[3] = now in seconds

local key = KEYS[1]
local window = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local max_requests = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])

local data = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'prev_count', 'curr_count', 'curr_window_start')
local prev_count = tonumber(data[1]) or 0
local curr_count = tonumber(data[2]) or 0
local curr_window_start = tonumber(data[3]) or now

-- Rotate window if needed
if now - curr_window_start >= window then
    prev_count = curr_count
    curr_count = 0
    curr_window_start = now
end

-- Weighted blend
local overlap = (window - (now - curr_window_start)) / window
local weighted_count = prev_count * overlap + curr_count

if weighted_count < max_requests then
    curr_count = curr_count + 1
    redis.call('HMSET', key, 'prev_count', prev_count, 'curr_count', curr_count, 'curr_window_start', curr_window_start)
    redis.call('EXPIRE', key, window * 2)
    return {1, max_requests - math.floor(weighted_count) - 1, 0}
end

return {0, 0, math.ceil(window * (1 - (weighted_count - max_requests) / max_requests))}

data.title: Sliding window middleware in C#
data.content: Use the approximate sliding window for production APIs.

data.title: Memory management
data.text: For the exact sorted set approach, set a TTL on the key equal to the window size. The ZREMRANGEBYSCORE command cleans expired entries on each request. Monitor Redis memory usage if you have millions of unique rate limit keys.

items.question: When should I use exact vs approximate?
items.answer: Use approximate for general API rate limiting. It is accurate enough and uses O(1) memory. Use exact only for compliance or billing systems where every request must be counted precisely.

items.question: Can I combine multiple algorithms?
items.answer: Yes. Use token bucket for burst tolerance and sliding window for long-term accuracy. Chain them: the request must pass both checks.

items.question: How do I handle multiple rate limit dimensions?
items.answer: Create separate Redis keys for each dimension: rate:user:123 (per user), rate:user:123:search (per user per endpoint), rate:ip:1.2.3.4 (per IP). Evaluate them in sequence.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Sliding window eliminates boundary burst with weighted counters.
Approximate is O(1) and 99% accurate — use it by default.
Exact sliding window stores all timestamps — use for billing/compliance.
Lua scripts make Redis operations atomic.
data.takeaway: Sliding window is the most accurate general-purpose rate limiter. Implement the approximate variant for production — it gives you accuracy without memory growth.
